Duration::floordiv¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Duration Duration::floordiv(std::int64_t k) const;

What It Does¶

Divides a Duration by a plain integer count k, flooring the underlying nanosecond count to the nearest whole nanosecond — the integer-division counterpart to div, which divides exactly. k divides the underlying nanosecond count directly, unit-agnostic like mul/div.

Parameters¶

k (std::int64_t)

A plain integer divisor, applied to the whole Duration (every element, if self is N-D).

Returns¶

Duration A new duration holding the elementwise, nanosecond-floored result.

Examples¶

Example 1. Floor-divide an array Duration by 3.

auto ranged = pluss::duration::range(
    pluss::duration::days(0), pluss::duration::days(10), pluss::duration::days(2));
std::cout << pluss::duration::print(ranged.floordiv(3));

Output¶

Duration(shape=[6], dim=1, numel=6)
[ 0 days 00:00:00.000000000, 0 days 16:00:00.000000000, 1 days 08:00:00.000000000, 2 days 00:00:00.000000000, 2 days 16:00:00.000000000, 3 days 08:00:00.000000000 ]

[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10] days each floor-divided by 3: 2 days / 3 lands on 0 days 16:00:00 (not a whole number of days), 4 days / 3 on 1 days 08:00:00, and so on — the flooring happens at nanosecond granularity, not at the whole-day level, which is exactly why the result isn’t itself a whole number of days.

Notes¶

  • floordiv floors at the nanosecond level, not at the level of whatever unit you read the result back through — a .total().days() reading can still show a non-integer number of days even though the underlying nanosecond count was floored exactly.

  • There is no Duration.floordiv(Duration) overload — see mul’s notes for why elapsed-time-times-elapsed-time isn’t representable here.

See Also¶

  • div: the exact (non-flooring) counterpart.

  • mod: the remainder complementary to this floor-division.

  • mul: scaling in the other direction.
